newsitem.title: UK: Fresh sleaze claims rock Major's re-election hopes.
newsitem.headline: Fresh sleaze claims rock Major's re-election hopes.

text.p: Political sleaze returned to haunt Britain's ruling Conservative party on Tuesday, just days before John Major launches a last-ditch campaign to secure his re-election as prime minister.

Former minister Neil Hamilton stopped a libel case against the Guardian on Monday and angrily denied fresh claims by the newspaper on Tuesday that he accepted cash for asking parliamentary questions. Hamilton said he was stopping his case only because he could not afford the legal fees.

The Guardian devoted three pages to Hamilton and his alleged activities and named four other Conservative MPs it said had earned "cash for questions" by lobbying in parliament on behalf of Mohammed al-Fayed, owner of London store Harrods.

Several other newspapers also made Hamilton their lead story, reminding electors of a history of sleaze allegations against the ruling Conservatives, who begin their pre-election party conference in exactly one week's time.

The allegations, ranging from MPs' sexual peccadillos through "cash for questions" to the way the party itself raises its funds, frustrated Major's efforts to drag the Conservatives out of the political abyss in 1994 and 1995.

But recent opinion polls have indicated that, helped by a booming economy, he has started to regain ground. A poll in Monday's Daily Telegraph said the opposition Labour Party's lead had dropped by six points to 27 in less than a month.
Major, who must call an election by next May, had agreed to give evidence to support Hamilton.
He will be relieved the four-week case will now no longer take the media spotlight away from his party's conference but the publicity surrounding it is still extremely embarrassing.

It has clouded his hopes that the conference will provide an opportunity to emphasise the positive message he can give on the economy and debunk Tony Blair's claim to have transformed Labour into a party that can govern successfully.
Opposition parties are determined to keep the sleaze issue running throughout Major's conference week.
Brian Wilson, a senior member of Labour's election campaign team, told BBC radio that the allegations against Hamilton were "of a devastating order for the Tory (Conservative) party".
"The idea that they can suppress them simply by getting rid of this court case...will just not be acceptable to parliament or indeed the electorate," he said.

Alex Carlile, a minority Liberal Democrat MP, called for parliament's Standards Committee to carry out a full investigation into allegations against Hamilton and others made by Egyptian-born al-Fayed.
"The committee...should call him to give evidence without restricting its scope to narrow specifics," he said.

Sixteen Conservative MPs have resigned from government posts following allegations of misconduct since Major unexpectedly steered his party to a fourth consecutive term of office at the 1992 general election.
To limit the political damage, Major set up a commission into standards of public life under judge Lord Michael Nolan.
But when parliament debated its report last November, Major opposed a call for all MPs to declare earnings from consultancy work in a parliamentary register open to public scrutiny.
He was defeated by 51 votes, giving opposition parties the chance to accuse him of being soft on political corruption.
